quests.title: Toy Box Time Machine
quests.story: You have found a dusty toy box in the attic! Some toys are very old and some are new. Can you tell them apart?
quests.instruction: Is the toy from long ago, or from now? Tap the right basket.
quests.hint: Does it need a screen, a battery or a charger? Old toys were made of wood, tin or cloth.

questions.ask: A wooden spinning top
questions.fact: Children have spun tops for thousands of years, even in Ancient Egypt.

questions.ask: A rocking horse
questions.fact: Wooden rocking horses were a favourite toy for Victorian children who had money to spare.

questions.ask: A tin soldier
questions.fact: Toy soldiers were made of tin or lead and painted by hand.

questions.ask: A peg doll
questions.fact: Peg dolls were made from wooden clothes pegs, with painted faces and scraps of cloth.

questions.ask: A hoop and a stick
questions.fact: Children raced along the street, tapping a big hoop with a stick to keep it rolling.

questions.ask: A wooden cup and ball
questions.fact: You swing the ball on its string and try to catch it in the cup. It is tricky!

questions.ask: A tablet with games on it
questions.fact: Tablet computers only became common in homes about 15 years ago.

questions.ask: A remote-control drone
questions.fact: Toy drones have spinning blades and fly using a battery and a radio controller.

questions.ask: A video game console
questions.fact: Video games plug into a TV, so they could not exist before televisions and computers.

questions.ask: A robot pet that talks
questions.fact: Talking robot toys use tiny computer chips to listen and answer you.

questions.ask: A toy you charge with a cable
questions.fact: Toys with batteries you can charge are new. Most old toys needed no power at all.

questions.ask: A virtual reality headset
questions.fact: A VR headset shows a screen to each eye, so it feels like you are inside a game.

quests.title: Grandma's Kitchen
quests.story: Step into a kitchen from long ago! There is no fridge and no washing machine. How did people get their jobs done?
quests.instruction: Read each question about old homes, then tap the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about whether it needs electricity. Most homes long ago did not have it.

questions.ask: What did people scrub clothes on long ago?
questions.fact: They rubbed wet, soapy clothes up and down its bumpy ridges to get them clean.

questions.ask: What did people use to squeeze wet clothes?
questions.fact: You turned a big handle, and the clothes were squashed between two rollers.

questions.ask: Where was food kept cool before fridges?
questions.fact: A larder was a cool cupboard or small room, often with a cold stone shelf.

questions.ask: What kept a home warm long ago?
questions.fact: Someone had to carry in coal and sweep out the ashes every day.

questions.ask: What gave light before electric lights?
questions.fact: Oil lamps had a wick that soaked up oil and burned with a small flame.

questions.ask: What did people hit a dusty rug with?
questions.fact: They hung the rug on a washing line outside and whacked the dust out of it.

questions.ask: What did many families have a bath in?
questions.fact: It was often put in front of the fire, and the family took turns in the same water.

questions.ask: What did people heat up to iron clothes?
questions.fact: It was warmed on the stove, so people used two and swapped them as one cooled.

questions.ask: What big black stove did people cook on?
questions.fact: A range had a fire, an oven and a hot plate all in one, and it warmed the kitchen.

questions.ask: Where was the toilet in many old homes?
questions.fact: Many homes had a toilet in the back yard. It was very chilly on winter nights!

questions.ask: Who brought milk to the door each day?
questions.fact: Milk came in glass bottles, and the milkman took the empty ones back to use again.

questions.ask: What do we use now instead of a mangle?
questions.fact: Washing machines did not become common in British homes until about 60 years ago.

quests.title: The School Bell Rings
quests.story: Ding-a-ling! The bell rings in an old Victorian classroom. Help the teacher sort school life long ago from school today.
quests.instruction: Is it from school long ago, or today? Tap the right book.
quests.hint: Think about your own classroom. Do you have that at school today?

questions.ask: Writing on a slate
questions.fact: A slate was a small board of grey stone. You could wipe it clean and use it again.

questions.ask: Dipping a pen in an ink well
questions.fact: Ink wells sat in a hole in the desk. Children had to be careful not to make blots!

questions.ask: Wearing a dunce's cap
questions.fact: A child could be made to wear a tall paper cap. Today we know that was unkind.

questions.ask: Boys and girls using separate doors
questions.fact: Some old schools still have the words Boys and Girls carved over two doors.

questions.ask: Standing up to answer the teacher
questions.fact: Children stood up straight and called the teacher Sir or Ma'am.

questions.ask: A class of 60 children
questions.fact: Victorian classes were huge, and older pupils often helped to teach the younger ones.

questions.ask: Learning on a tablet
questions.fact: Tablets can show videos, games and books all on one screen.

questions.ask: A whiteboard you can touch
questions.fact: An interactive whiteboard is a big computer screen the whole class can see.

questions.ask: Boys and girls playing together
questions.fact: Today boys and girls learn and play together in the same class.

questions.ask: The register on a computer
questions.fact: Long ago the teacher wrote the register in a big book with a pen.

questions.ask: Watching a video in class
questions.fact: Videos need screens and electricity, which Victorian schools did not have.

questions.ask: Seat belts on the school coach
questions.fact: Seat belts on coaches keep you safe on school trips. Victorian children mostly walked.

quests.title: Seaside Snapshots

skill.name: Seaside holidays long ago and now
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Look at these old seaside photos! Find out what a day at the beach was like long ago, and how it has changed.
quests.instruction: Read each seaside question, then tap the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about what people had long ago. There were no phones, planes or screens.

questions.ask: How did families get to the sea long ago?
questions.fact: In Victorian times, new railways made cheap day trips to the seaside possible.

questions.ask: What hut on wheels took people into the sea?
questions.fact: Horses pulled it into the water so people could get changed and step into the sea.

questions.ask: Which puppet show was on the beach?
questions.fact: Punch and Judy shows have been on British beaches for well over 100 years.

questions.ask: Which animal could you ride on the sand?
questions.fact: Donkey rides are still on some British beaches today.

questions.ask: What is a long walkway out over the sea?
questions.fact: Southend Pier is over 2 kilometres long, the longest pleasure pier in the world.

questions.ask: What did people sit on to rest on the sand?
questions.fact: Deckchairs fold flat, and people paid a few pennies to hire one for the day.

questions.ask: What were old swimsuits made of?
questions.fact: Woolly swimsuits covered arms and legs, and got heavy and saggy when wet!

questions.ask: What took seaside snaps long ago?
questions.fact: You had to wait days for the photos to be printed before you could see them.

questions.ask: How do lots of families get to the sea now?
questions.fact: Today many families also fly to beaches in other countries, which was rare long ago.

questions.ask: Which sweet has words all the way through?
questions.fact: Seaside rock with letters running through it has been made since Victorian times.

questions.ask: What new days off began in 1871?
questions.fact: Bank holidays gave workers a free day, so many went on a trip to the seaside.

questions.ask: What do we put on now to stop sunburn?
questions.fact: Long ago, people kept out of the sun with big hats and parasols instead.

quests.title: Wheels Through Time
quests.story: Beep beep! Clip clop! All sorts of transport are rolling down the country road. Help put them in time order.
quests.instruction: Tap the kind of transport that came first.
quests.hint: Did it need an engine? Animals and wind came first, then steam, then engines and jets.

events.label: The first wheels
events.fact: The first wheels were solid wood, made about 5,500 years ago in Mesopotamia.

events.label: Horse and chariot
events.fact: Chariots had light wheels with spokes, so horses could pull them very fast.

events.label: Stagecoach
events.fact: Stagecoaches pulled by horses carried people from town to town, swapping horses on the way.

events.label: Hot-air balloon
events.fact: The first people to fly rode in a hot-air balloon made by the Montgolfier brothers in France.

events.label: Steam train
events.fact: Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first steam passenger train on a public railway in England.

events.label: Penny-farthing bike
events.fact: The penny-farthing had a giant front wheel and a tiny back one, like two old coins.

events.label: First motor car
events.fact: Karl Benz built a car with three wheels and an engine that burned petrol.

events.label: First aeroplane
events.fact: The Wright brothers' plane flew for just 12 seconds on its first flight.

events.label: Jet airliner
events.fact: The British Comet was the first jet airliner to carry passengers.

events.label: Moon rocket
events.fact: A giant rocket called Saturn V carried astronauts all the way to the Moon.

quests.title: The Lamplighter's Night

skill.name: How we made light through time
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Night is falling, and the lamplighter needs your help! Light up the street by putting ways of making light in time order.
quests.instruction: Tap the way of making light that came first.
quests.hint: Flames came first, then gas, then electricity. Which one needs a plug or a battery?

events.label: Campfire
events.fact: People have used fire for light and warmth for hundreds of thousands of years.

events.label: Stone fat lamp
events.fact: Stone Age people burned animal fat in hollow stones to light up dark caves.

events.label: Clay oil lamp
events.fact: Small clay lamps burned olive oil or other oils through a wick.

events.label: Candle
events.fact: The Romans made candles from beeswax or animal fat, called tallow.

events.label: Gas street lamp
events.fact: Pall Mall in London got gas street lamps. Lamplighters lit them every evening.

events.label: Electric light bulb
events.fact: Joseph Swan in England and Thomas Edison in America both made light bulbs that worked.

events.label: Battery torch
events.fact: The first torches had weak batteries, so they only gave short flashes of light.

events.label: Neon sign
events.fact: Neon gas glows bright red-orange when electricity passes through it.

events.label: First LED light
events.fact: The first LEDs glowed red and were tiny, used as lights on machines.

events.label: LED bulbs at home
events.fact: LED bulbs use much less electricity than old bulbs and last for years.

quests.title: Grace Darling's Rescue
quests.story: Wind howls round the lighthouse and waves crash on the rocks! Find out how brave Grace Darling helped people in danger.
quests.instruction: Read each question about Grace, then tap the right answer.
quests.hint: Picture the lighthouse on its rocky island in a storm. What would Grace see and use?

questions.ask: Where did Grace Darling live?
questions.fact: Grace lived in the Longstone Lighthouse, on a rocky island out at sea.

questions.ask: What was her dad's job?
questions.fact: William Darling kept the lamp burning so ships could see the rocks at night.

questions.ask: What hit the rocks in the storm?
questions.fact: The steamship Forfarshire hit a rock called Big Harcar and broke in two.

questions.ask: In what year was the rescue?
questions.fact: The rescue was early in the morning on 7 September 1838.

questions.ask: How did Grace get to the people?
questions.fact: The rowing boat was called a coble, and the waves were very big.

questions.ask: Who rowed with Grace?
questions.fact: Grace kept the boat steady while her dad helped people off the rock.

questions.ask: How many people did they save?
questions.fact: They took some people back to the lighthouse, and her dad went back for the rest.

questions.ask: What was the weather like?
questions.fact: Strong winds and huge waves made the rescue very dangerous.

questions.ask: How old was Grace?
questions.fact: Grace was 22, and soon people all over Britain knew her name.

questions.ask: Which islands is her lighthouse on?
questions.fact: The Farne Islands are off the coast of Northumberland, and puffins and seals live there.

questions.ask: Who sent Grace a gift of money?
questions.fact: Queen Victoria sent her £50, and lots of people sent letters, poems and gifts.

questions.ask: Where is the museum about Grace?
questions.fact: The RNLI Grace Darling Museum in Bamburgh has the boat she rowed in the rescue.

quests.title: The Lady with the Lamp
quests.story: A soft light glows in the hospital at night. Meet Florence Nightingale, the nurse who changed hospitals for ever!
quests.instruction: Read each question about Florence, then tap the right answer.
quests.hint: Remember that Florence was a nurse who wanted sick people to get well in clean places.

questions.ask: What was Florence's job?
questions.fact: In 1820, when Florence was born, nursing was not seen as a proper job for a rich girl.

questions.ask: What was Florence called?
questions.fact: A newspaper gave her this name after she checked on soldiers at night.

questions.ask: Which city was she named after?
questions.fact: She was born in the city of Florence in Italy, while her English family was there.

questions.ask: Who did Florence help in the war?
questions.fact: She cared for British soldiers who were hurt or ill in the Crimean War.

questions.ask: Which country was her hospital in?
questions.fact: Her hospital was at Scutari, which is now part of the city of Istanbul.

questions.ask: How many nurses went with her?
questions.fact: She set off in 1854 with 38 nurses to the army hospital.

questions.ask: What was the hospital like when she came?
questions.fact: There were rats, dirty sheets and not enough food or soap.

questions.ask: What did Florence do to help?
questions.fact: Her nurses scrubbed floors, washed sheets and cooked better food.

questions.ask: What did she carry on her night rounds?
questions.fact: Her lamp was a Turkish lantern, which folded up like a paper concertina.

questions.ask: What did Florence draw to share her ideas?
questions.fact: Her clever charts showed that clean hospitals saved lives.

questions.ask: What did she start in London in 1860?
questions.fact: The Nightingale School at St Thomas' Hospital trained nurses for many years.

questions.ask: Which day is now Nurses Day?
questions.fact: International Nurses Day is on 12 May, the day Florence was born.

quests.title: Castle Explorers
quests.story: Lower the drawbridge! You are exploring a castle. Find out what each part was for and who lived there.
quests.instruction: Read each castle question, then tap the right answer.
quests.hint: Castles were built to keep people safe. Think about how each part helped keep enemies out.

questions.ask: What is the water around a castle?
questions.fact: A moat made it hard for enemies to reach the walls.

questions.ask: Which bridge can be pulled up?
questions.fact: Chains pulled the drawbridge up so no one could cross the moat.

questions.ask: What is the big strong tower called?
questions.fact: The keep was the safest place in the castle, where the lord often lived.

questions.ask: What metal gate drops down?
questions.fact: A portcullis was a heavy grid of wood and iron that slid down to block the gate.

questions.ask: What are the bumpy tops of the walls?
questions.fact: Guards could hide behind the high parts and look out through the gaps.

questions.ask: Where did everyone eat a big feast?
questions.fact: The great hall had long tables, a big fire and sometimes music.

questions.ask: Who was in charge of the castle?
questions.fact: The lord and lady ran the castle and the land around it.

questions.ask: Who wore armour and rode a horse?
questions.fact: A knight trained for years, starting as a young page.

questions.ask: Who told jokes to make the lord laugh?
questions.fact: Jesters wore bright clothes and hats with bells, and juggled and sang.

questions.ask: What were the first Norman castles made of?
questions.fact: After 1066 the Normans built wooden castles quickly, then rebuilt many in stone.

questions.ask: Who looked out of the thin window slits?
questions.fact: The slits were thin on the outside, so archers inside stayed safe.

questions.ask: Which castle is a home for the King?
questions.fact: Windsor Castle is the oldest and largest castle in the world that people still live in.

quests.title: Past and Present Detectives

skill.name: Words about time and the past
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Welcome to the museum, detective! Use clues and time words to find out about the past.
quests.instruction: Read each detective question, then tap the right answer.
quests.hint: Past means before now, present means now, and future means after now.

questions.ask: Which words mean long ago?
questions.fact: History is the story of the past, from yesterday to thousands of years ago.

questions.ask: Which words mean now?
questions.fact: The present is the time we are in right now.

questions.ask: Which words mean after now?
questions.fact: Nobody knows the future yet, but we can make plans for it.

questions.ask: What day came just before today?
questions.fact: Today will be yesterday when you wake up tomorrow!

questions.ask: Where can you see very old things?
questions.fact: Museums keep old things safe so everyone can learn from them.

questions.ask: Who is the oldest?
questions.fact: Great-grandma is your grandma's or grandad's mum.

questions.ask: Who can tell us about the past?
questions.fact: Older people remember what life was like when they were young.

questions.ask: What shows how Grandad looked as a boy?
questions.fact: Photos are clues that show us clothes, toys and homes from the past.

questions.ask: What colours are many very old photos?
questions.fact: Most family photos were black and white until about 60 years ago.

questions.ask: What shows events in time order?
questions.fact: A timeline puts the oldest things at one end and the newest at the other.

questions.ask: What do we call 100 years?
questions.fact: A decade is 10 years, and a century is 100 years.

questions.ask: Who digs up old things from long ago?
questions.fact: Archaeologists use small trowels and brushes so they don't break what they find.
